title: Paediatric dehydration
description: A mother brings her 14-month-old son, who has vomiting and diarrhoea and is difficult to wake.

speaker.name: Lerato Dlamini
speaker.role: the mother and caregiver of the patient
speaker.style: Worried, cooperative, and tired. She sometimes uses home remedies and may not understand medical terms. She becomes tearful when describing how sleepy her child is.

patient.name: Tshepo Dlamini
patient.living_situation: Lives with his mother, father, and older sibling

presenting_complaint: Two days of diarrhoea and vomiting, poor drinking, very few wet nappies, and unusual sleepiness.
opening_line: Sister, Tshepo has been vomiting and having diarrhoea since yesterday. He is very sleepy and has not made a wet nappy since last night.
personality: Worried and protective. She answers questions carefully and appreciates clear explanations. She may minimise how little he has been drinking if she feels judged.

history.onset: Watery diarrhoea started two days ago. Vomiting started yesterday and has become more frequent.
history.stools: Six to eight watery stools today. No blood or mucus in the stool.
history.vomiting: About five episodes since this morning. He cannot keep water or breast milk down.
history.feeding: Breastfeeding much less than usual. He refuses food and has not drunk from a cup today.
history.urine_output: No wet nappy for more than ten hours. The last nappy was only slightly wet.
history.hydration_signs: His eyes look sunken to his mother, he has no tears when crying, and his mouth looks dry.
history.alertness: He is unusually sleepy and floppy. He wakes briefly when spoken to but goes back to sleep.
history.fever: He felt hot at home. The mother thinks his temperature was 38.4 degrees Celsius.
history.past_medical_history: Born at term. No chronic illness. No previous hospital admissions.
history.medications: No chronic medication. The mother gave a little paracetamol yesterday.
history.social_history: Lives in a rural village with both parents and an older sibling. The older sibling had a similar illness last week. The family has limited transport to the clinic.
history.weight: His mother thinks he last weighed about 9 kilograms.

risk_factors: two days of diarrhoea and vomiting
no wet nappy for more than ten hours

ground_truth.diagnosis: Severe dehydration due to acute gastroenteritis, with warning signs
red_flags: reduced urine output for more than eight hours
expected_actions: assess airway, breathing, circulation, and level of consciousness
weigh the child and check vital signs, capillary refill, and glucose if available
classify dehydration using a recognised paediatric protocol such as WHO or IMCI
start oral rehydration solution, nasogastric fluids, or intravenous fluids according to severity and local protocol
urgently refer or admit a child with severe dehydration or warning signs
continue breastfeeding and add zinc according to local guidance
avoid anti-diarrhoeal medicines and avoid giving plain water only
give clear safety-netting advice and arrange follow-up

vitals.result: Weight 9.0 kg. Capillary refill 3 seconds. Blood glucose 4.2 mmol/L. Eyes sunken, no tears, dry mucous membranes.

ecg.unavailable_reason: An ECG is not indicated in this dehydrated child; focus on ABCDE, hydration and urgent transfer.
ecg.result: An ECG is not indicated in this child.

oxygen.result: Oxygen started at 1-2 L/min via nasal prongs.

aspirin.warning: Aspirin is contraindicated in a child with a possible viral illness because of the risk of Reye syndrome.

iv_access.result: IV cannula sited. A 20 mL/kg crystalloid bolus was started per protocol, and bloods including glucose were taken.

call_ambulance.result: Emergency ambulance requested for urgent transfer to hospital. Estimated arrival 20 minutes.

escalate_doctor.result: Doctor informed using SBAR. Urgent paediatric review and transfer arranged.

red_flags.flag: Reduced urine output for more than eight hours

hints: Ask how long he has been unwell, how many stools and vomits, and whether he is drinking.
Wet nappies, tears, eyes and alertness are the key dehydration signs. Ask about each one directly.
He is lethargic and not keeping fluids down. Check observations and glucose, then plan IV fluids and urgent transfer.
Reassess after fluids and explain the plan to his mother in plain language, with clear safety-netting.

ideal_approach: Assess ABCDE, level of consciousness, and immediate danger signs in the child.
Weigh the child and record observations, capillary refill, temperature and blood glucose if available.
Ask specifically about stools, vomiting, drinking, wet nappies, tears, eyes, mouth and alertness.
Classify dehydration using WHO or IMCI criteria and recognise severe dehydration with warning signs.
Secure IV access and start isotonic fluids per protocol; use nasogastric oral rehydration if IV access is delayed and the child is not in shock.
Arrange urgent transfer or admission. Continue breastfeeding and give zinc according to local guidance.
Avoid anti-diarrhoeal medicines and plain water only; give clear safety-netting and follow-up advice to the mother.
debrief.model_answer: Tshepo is a 14-month-old boy weighing about 9 kg, with two days of watery diarrhoea and vomiting, no wet nappy for more than ten hours, and unusual sleepiness and floppiness. He has sunken eyes, no tears and a dry mouth, and his temperature is 38.4 C. Observations show HR 150, BP 85/50, RR 40 and capillary refill of 3 seconds. This is severe dehydration with warning signs, likely due to acute gastroenteritis. Immediate priorities are ABCDE, glucose, IV access and isotonic fluid resuscitation per protocol, urgent transfer to hospital, continued breastfeeding and zinc where appropriate. Avoid anti-diarrhoeal medicines and plain water only. Explain the plan to his mother and give clear safety-netting.
reflection_questions: Which clinical signs told you this child was severely dehydrated rather than mildly dehydrated?
Why are anti-diarrhoeal medicines and plain water alone unsafe in this child?
How did you explain the urgency to his mother, and what did you check that she understood?
references: World Health Organization. Pocket Book of Hospital Care for Children. 2nd edition.
World Health Organization and UNICEF. Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) chart booklet. Latest edition.
National Department of Health. Standard Treatment Guidelines and Essential Medicines List for South Africa: Paediatric Hospital Level. Latest edition.

learning_objectives: Assess a child for dehydration using a structured approach
Recognise danger signs in a lethargic child
Choose an appropriate rehydration and referral plan
Communicate clearly with a worried caregiver and check understanding
